title: The World Cup Comes to Silicon Valley. For NRIs in the Bay Area, It's Already Home.
excerpt: The USA face Bosnia and Herzegovina at Levi's Stadium on Wednesday — and for the half-million Indian Americans living within driving distance, football's biggest party is unfolding in their own backyard.
body:
The World Cup is in California. And for the Indian diaspora in the San Francisco Bay Area — one of the densest concentrations of NRIs anywhere on the planet — Wednesday's Round of 32 clash between the United States and Bosnia and Herzegovina at Levi's Stadium isn't just another game on FOX. It's a moment that's been decades in the making.

Kickoff is at 5 PM Pacific on July 1. The venue sits in Santa Clara, surrounded by the tech campuses of Apple, Google, Intel, and a hundred startups, in a region that is home to more than 500,000 Indian Americans. For a community that grew up on cricket and only slowly adopted the beautiful game through their children's rec leagues and EPL-obsessed college friends, a World Cup knockout match 20 minutes from their Cupertino living rooms feels almost surreal.

## How the USA Got Here

The U.S. Men's National Team topped Group D with two convincing wins before stumbling in the final game. A ruthless 4-1 demolition of Paraguay at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood on opening day set the tone, followed by a disciplined 2-0 shutout of Australia in Seattle. The loss to Turkey — a chaotic 3-2 affair at SoFi — didn't matter for qualification but raised questions about defensive vulnerability that head coach Mauricio Pochettino will need to address.

Christian Pulisic, the AC Milan playmaker, remains the heartbeat of this squad. Tyler Adams and Weston McKennie anchor a midfield that has controlled possession in every group match, while Malik Tillman — Bayer Leverkusen's gifted 24-year-old — has emerged as the creative fulcrum. The frontline of Folarin Balogun and Tim Weah gives the U.S. a blend of pace and technical quality that few teams in the tournament can match on the counterattack.

Several regular starters who sat out the Turkey match are expected to return, and the squad will be eager to restore momentum at a venue where they'll have near-universal crowd support.

## Bosnia's Quiet Credibility

Bosnia and Herzegovina should not be underestimated. Qualifying for the knockout stage of a 48-team World Cup is no small feat for a nation of 3.2 million, and their group-stage performances earned them passage through one of the tournament's more competitive pools. They carry the legacy of the 2014 World Cup — their first — and a deeply motivated squad that plays with pride and tactical intelligence.

Their key dangerman, Edin Džeko, may be in the twilight of his career, but he remains a clinical finisher with vast experience at the highest levels. Bosnia's midfield is combative and well-organised, and they won't be fazed by a hostile road atmosphere in Santa Clara.

## The Bay Area's World Cup Surprise

The Bay Area was supposed to be the tournament's sleepy afterthought. When the fixture list dropped, social media ranked Santa Clara as the least glamorous host city. No Messi. No Mbappé. No Brazil. The highest-ranked visitor across five group-stage matches was 16th-ranked Switzerland.

"The World Cup was supposed to be a Bay Area bonanza. Why does it feel like a flop?" the San Francisco Chronicle asked before the tournament.

The narrative has reversed completely. More than 350,000 people have visited the fan zone at San Pedro Square in San Jose since the tournament began. The lowest attendance at Levi's Stadium was 67,966 — a few hundred short of full capacity. For the USA match, organisers have added a fourth giant screen at the fan zone, and resale tickets on StubHub have spiked past $2,000 for the cheapest seats.

Levi's Stadium itself scored a 7.48 out of 10 in a SeatPick fan-experience ranking — fifth among all 11 U.S. venues — with pleasant June weather, moderate beer prices, and low mosquito risk playing in its favour.

## Cricket Country Goes to Football

For the South Asian diaspora, the Bay Area's World Cup story has a particular resonance. This is a community that built cricket leagues in Sunnyvale parks and stayed up past midnight to watch IPL matches streamed from India. Football was always the second sport — something the kids played in Fremont recreational leagues, something colleagues in the office talked about during Champions League weeks.

But the World Cup changes everything. When the biggest sporting event in the world sets up 15 minutes from your office, tribal affiliations expand. Indian-American families who wouldn't dream of watching an MLS game are buying tickets, painting their faces in red, white, and blue, and debating Pochettino's back line with the same intensity they'd usually reserve for an India-Pakistan series.

"I follow European football, so for sure, I was disappointed — I would have liked more balance in the teams we got here," one Bay Area resident told Reuters at a group-stage match at the stadium. "But having a World Cup here is fantastic. There was no way I was going to miss it."

The broader point is hard to miss: NRIs in the United States are, in meaningful and growing numbers, becoming American football fans — not the kind with shoulder pads and helmets, but the kind that FIFA governs. The U.S. men's team, packed with young talent playing across Europe's top leagues, is accessible and exciting in a way it has never been before. And for immigrants who chose this country, there is a quiet emotional pull to cheering for it.

## What's at Stake

A win sends the USA to the Round of 16 — a stage they reached in Qatar in 2022 — with a likely quarterfinal in Los Angeles if they keep advancing. A loss ends the dream of a deep home-tournament run. For the first time since 1994, the World Cup is on American soil, and Wednesday's match is the last group- or knockout-stage fixture in the Bay Area before the calendar turns to a single quarterfinal at SoFi on July 10.

For NRIs watching from the stands in Santa Clara or from their couches in Sunnyvale, Milpitas, and Fremont, the match carries an extra weight. It's proof that their adopted country is part of the global game. It's proof that Santa Clara — a city that barely had a bar scene before Levi's Stadium was built — can host the biggest show on earth. And it's proof that the World Cup, like everything else, belongs to whoever shows up.

Kickoff is at 5 PM Pacific on FOX. The Bay Area, once derided as the World Cup's quietest corner, will be anything but quiet.

- **Venue:** Levi's Stadium, Santa Clara, California
